title: Pressure-cooker oatmeal
subtitle: Creamy, no-stir porridge in 3 minutes
excerpt: Rolled oats cooked under pressure into a smooth, creamy porridge. The pressure breaks down the oat structure evenly, producing a result far better than stovetop porridge without any stirring.
sourceNotes: Pressure-cooker porridge became widely documented after the rise of electric pressure cooker recipe communities in the 2010s. The method applies pressure to soften oats in a fraction of the usual stovetop time.

recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch, portion into containers, refrigerate for up to 4 days, and reheat with a splash of milk.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Reheat portions with a splash of milk over medium heat, stirring until smooth.

content.text: Pressure-cooker oatmeal takes 3 minutes at pressure and produces a creamier, smoother result than stovetop porridge cooked for 10 minutes. The pressure breaks down the oat structure evenly and gelatinises the starch without any stirring. It also makes a large batch efficiently, cook four portions and reheat across the week.

Use rolled oats, not instant oats, instant oats become gluey under pressure. Steel-cut oats produce a chewier, nuttier porridge and need a longer cook time (see the separate steel-cut oats entry). For rolled oats, 3 minutes at pressure is exactly right.
Oatmeal can foam significantly during pressure cooking. Do not fill the pot more than halfway, and always use a natural pressure release, a quick release can push foam through the valve.

Put the rolled oats, {{whole-milk}} of whole milk, and salt into the pressure cooker. Stir once to combine. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 3 minutes. Allow a full natural pressure release, do not quick-release, as oatmeal foam can block the valve.

Open the lid and stir, the oatmeal will look thick on top and loose underneath. Stir vigorously to combine into a uniform creamy porridge. If too thick, stir in a splash of warm milk. Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed. Serve with honey, fruit, or cream.

rows.symptom: Oatmeal has spattered from the pressure valve
rows.cause: The pot was overfilled, or quick-release was used.
rows.fix: Never fill the pot more than half full for porridge. Always use natural release. Clean the valve thoroughly before the next use.

rows.cause: The oats clumped before the pressure built.
rows.fix: Stir vigorously after opening. For the next batch, stir the oats and milk together before sealing.

rows.cause: Rolled oats vary in how much liquid they absorb.
rows.fix: Stir in a splash of hot milk or water until it loosens to the consistency you prefer.

content.text: Porridge is a Scottish and northern English tradition. The classic version is plain, with just a pinch of salt. The modern version adds honey, cream, or fruit. The pressure cooker makes batch cooking easy. Cook four portions on Sunday and reheat each morning with a splash of milk.
